title: 'Is this a cyberattack?' Grounded flights, a Microsoft outage and AI chaos fuel cybersecurity fears
summary: A series of unsettling disruptions, from tech stock turbulence and Microsoft outages to a nationwide grounding of flights, has left millions wondering whether the world’s increasingly interconnected technology systems are beginning to unravel.
author: FRANCE 24

title: Arthur Mensch and Mistral AI: what does it take to keep a model in European hands?
summary: An organisation may want to run a powerful model close to the people whose records it processes. Mistral offers one route: release weights that can be deployed under the customer’s control, and sell the infrastructure and expertise needed to operate them. Arthur Mensch’s French company gives Europe a stake in frontier research. Its training hardware and industrial shareholders show how international that undertaking remains.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Zhilin Yang and Moonshot AI: who can promise capacity for Kimi?
summary: A subscription buys access to a model only while the service can answer. When demand for Kimi outstripped the available computing capacity, Moonshot paused new subscriptions. That episode illuminates founder Zhilin Yang’s two jobs. One is to improve a language model. The other is to secure the machines and capital to deliver it to the people who have paid for it.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Dayiheng Liu and Qwen: who steers the model inside Alibaba?
summary: A developer can download some Qwen models, rent others by the token and run either on infrastructure supplied by Alibaba. Three decisions lie behind that apparent choice. The researchers decide what to train, the cloud business decides what to sell and the parent company decides where capital goes. Dayiheng Liu’s career shows how much influence a technical leader can exercise within that structure and where his authority ends.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Alex Karp and the software between the model and the decision
summary: An AI supplier can shape a decision without training the model that produced the answer. Palantir links data, permissions and actions inside institutions. Alex Karp’s influence is easiest to see at the point where an analyst’s suggestion becomes something a hospital, factory or government agency can actually do.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Dario Amodei and the terms on which Anthropic can go public
summary: Anthropic promises to consider the long-term effects of the systems it builds. A proposed stock offering brings that promise into contact with shareholders seeking a return. Who can vote, who can appoint directors and who supplies the computing capacity each tell a different part of Dario Amodei’s story.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Elon Musk and the connection between satellites, servers and AI
summary: A customer can ask Grok a question over a Starlink connection. Parts of that journey now belong to the same listed group. Following the money from rockets and satellite subscriptions to servers explains why SpaceX belongs in a discussion about AI, and why its share price tells only part of the story.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Satya Nadella and Microsoft’s place on both sides of an AI purchase
summary: A company buying an AI assistant may already buy its office software, identity service and cloud capacity from Microsoft. Satya Nadella helped build the cloud business before he became chief executive. His position matters wherever a customer must decide how easily one part of that bundle can be replaced.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Sam Altman and the question of who controls OpenAI
summary: Who gets to appoint the board of a company that builds frontier AI? Sam Altman runs OpenAI, Microsoft owns an economic interest and a nonprofit holds governing rights. Following those three strands helps explain how a model can change a market without its chief executive owning that market.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Mark Zuckerberg and the votes behind Meta’s AI strategy
summary: A shareholder may own part of Meta and still have little say over the next generation of its AI. Mark Zuckerberg’s voting majority connects decisions about models, data centres and the distribution of information to one founder. The company’s public filings show exactly how that majority works.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Sundar Pichai and the routes through which Google brings AI to the public
summary: A model can reach millions before anyone chooses it by name. At Alphabet, Sundar Pichai oversees the researchers who build Gemini, the infrastructure that runs it and the products through which people encounter its answers. Google’s founders retain voting power that the chief executive himself does not possess.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Colette Kress and the board that chose NVIDIA’s interim chief
summary: When a founder leaves, who gets to choose a successor? At NVIDIA the answer arrived in a securities filing. The board appointed its finance chief, Colette Kress, to run the company while it searches for a permanent chief executive. It gave someone else the chair.
author: The Bible of AI

title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
summary: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet. Continue reading...

title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.

title: Landing to Raw to Bronze or straight from Landing to Bronze?
summary: tl;dr: I am currently working on building my personal data lake and medallion + platinum pipeline and need help deciding whether to have an Landing zone to Raw to Bronze steps for ingesting data or go directly to Bronze from the Landing zone. Context: I am working on a quantfied_self project where i am collecting a bunch of data on myself. Things like (everything is timestamped): - Location at all points in the day, - Every single workout set - Major actions i do during a day like brushing teeth, reading a book, meals, work, socialising etc etc etc - Financial transactions - Hourly health metrics like heart rate, Hrv, steps, energy spent, calorie intake etc etc etc - And a lot of other data. Again everything is timestamped so can be watermarked easily. The plan: The plan is to build my own local data platform where i upload / send the data and it runs PySpark transformations on the data through a medallion architecture and i can use the gold/platinum datasets for visualisations and getting insights into my behaviour patterns. What I currently have: - An old laptop that i have converted to a ubuntu server (with GUI) to be used for storage and compute. - Samba is setup and I have automated data transfer to the exposed “incoming” folder using automations that can run automatically or on demand. - The repo is set up and a cron job inside the repo runs the pipelines on schedule on the server. - Current architecture: Data collection (csv or json) -> auto save via automations to “/incoming/health” or “/incoming/financial” or “/incoming/gps” etc etc folders. title: Zig versus Rust and C++: who decides where the memory goes?
summary: Bun chose Zig and later moved to Rust. The team building the Roc compiler went the other way. What did each see that the other could afford to live without? Their accounts, a working terminal and a timed comparison with C++ reveal where Zig gives a team control over memory, and which mistakes the team must catch for itself.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Goose versus Rust and C++: the case for keeping data in place
summary: Goose lets a growing array keep its address and a whole group of objects disappear when their work is done. Wouter van Oortmerssen’s language turns those ideas into measurable savings on some workloads. The gap narrows when Rust and C++ use equally careful layouts. We follow the designer from Amiga compilers to FlatBuffers, examine how Claude Fable helped build Goose, and read the figures behind its strongest claims.

title: Diamond beyond silicon: what Ōkuma and boron compounds mean for AI chips

Its starting point was a practical problem: how do you keep instruments working where radiation makes the electronics difficult to replace? The need arose during the decommissioning of Fukushima Daiichi. It did not begin […]
author: The Bible of AI

title: Martin Davis and the Logic of a Checkable Plan
summary: Martin Davis spent much of his life asking which questions a machine could settle. As a student in New York, he took up a problem about equations that would occupy him for decades. In 1962 he and two colleagues described a machine that could pursue a line of reasoning, recognise a contradiction and retrieve an earlier decision from magnetic tape. That work helped establish a method for finding out whether a set of logical conditions can all hold at once. Decades later, researchers in artificial intelligence used that question to find plans. A sequence of actions had to lead from a stated starting point to a goal while obeying the rules at every step. Davis’s career offers a way to understand both the force of a proof and the care needed in deciding what, exactly, has been proved.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Graydon Hoare, Rust and the Broken Elevator
summary: In 2006 a broken elevator left Graydon Hoare with a long walk up to his Vancouver apartment. Years later, the Canadian engineer recalled the climb when he wrote about Rust, the programming language he had begun in his spare time at Mozilla. An old annoyance helps explain what he wanted from software. The route from his first experiments to a language people could depend on ran through the work of many others. A browser engine gave the team somewhere to test its ideas. A promise of stability gave users a reason to commit. Today, one can follow that history into an unexpected place. Before a language model processes a sentence, a tool has to break the text into units the model recognises. At Hugging Face, one widely available tool for that job has its core in Rust.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Leopold Aschenbrenner and the Case for AGI by 2027
summary: At fourteen, Leopold Aschenbrenner and a schoolmate built a system to measure fine particles in Berlin’s air. Eight years later, he published a forecast about machines that might soon do his own job. Between those projects came economics at Columbia, research on growth and catastrophic risk, and an experiment at OpenAI in which a weaker model helped train a stronger one. His June 2024 essay, Situational Awareness, asked what would happen if artificial intelligence could take over the work of an AI researcher. This profile follows that question into the laboratory, the electricity grid and the investment firm he helped bring into being. Evidence from 2026 gives different answers to different parts of his argument. Researchers have measured faster progress inside one laboratory. The prospect of a machine independently carrying a research programme from question to discovery remains open.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Aravind Srinivas and Perplexity: who chooses the sources behind an answer?
summary: A list of blue links lets the reader choose which account to open. An answer engine makes that decision once before the reader gets there. Aravind Srinivas built Perplexity around that exchange. Its citations can make research faster, but the order of the sources, the passages the system leaves out and the model used to assemble them all shape what the reader takes away.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Liang Wenfeng and DeepSeek: what did the famous training bill actually buy?
summary: One of the most consequential figures attached to DeepSeek was a dollar amount. Readers could reasonably ask whether a small laboratory had reproduced the work of much larger companies for less than six million dollars. Founder Liang Wenfeng’s history in quantitative finance explains where some of the machinery came from. The training paper explains which work the figure covers. Both are needed to understand what other laboratories might reproduce.
author: The Bible of AI

title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial
summary: Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “ reactive and risk-averse ” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?” This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “ human bandwidth ”. That is an extraordinary claim. Technology can help speed up identifying someone at risk of homelessness – but it does not supply a home. Better administration and adequate resources need each other. Continue reading...

title: Is the AI job apocalypse finally here? The evidence suggests otherwise | John Quiggin
summary: The role AI played in job losses at Australia’s NAB, Qantas, Canva and Atlassian is far from clear – but it may prove to have more impact on the stock market than the jobs market Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast In 1987, the Nobel prize winning economist Robert Solow remarked: “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” At the time, computers had been around for 40 years. Real productivity gains did emerge in the 1990s after the arrival of the internet, but they were short-lived. Four years after the launch of ChatGPT, the pattern seems to be much the same: lots of hype and excitement but with very little productivity growth. The main economic impacts, as in the 1990s dotcom era, have been a stock market boom and huge investment in infrastructure (fibre optics then, datacentres today), betting on future demand that has yet to emerge.
